# fpp3 3.7, Ex 1

> Consider the GDP information in `global_economy`.
> Plot the GDP per capita for each country over time.
> Which country has the highest GDP per capita?
> How has this changed over time?

```{r}
#| label: gdp_per_capita

global_economy |>
  autoplot(GDP / Population, alpha = 0.3) +
  guides(colour = "none") # turn off the legend else hard to see as there are many series
```

There are too many countries to use a legend, so we find the countries with the highest average GDP per capita, along with each country's most recent value.

```{r}
avg_gdp_pc <- global_economy |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Country) |>
  summarise(
    # Average GDP per capita for each country
    gdp_pc = mean(GDP / Population, na.rm = TRUE),
    # Most recent GDP per capita for each country
    last = last((GDP / Population)[!is.na(GDP / Population)])
  )
top_n(avg_gdp_pc, 5, gdp_pc)
```

Now we highlight the country with the highest average GDP per capita (Monaco), and label the five countries with the highest recent values.

```{r}
max_gdp_pc <- global_economy |>
  semi_join(
    avg_gdp_pc |>
      filter(gdp_pc == max(gdp_pc, na.rm = TRUE)),
    by = "Country"
  )
```

```{r}
library(ggrepel)
global_economy |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Year, y = GDP / Population, group = Country)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = "red", data = max_gdp_pc) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(label = Country, x = 2020, y = last),
    data = top_n(avg_gdp_pc, 5, last),
  )
```

Which country had the highest GDP per capita in each year?

```{r}
global_economy |>
  mutate(gdp_pc = GDP / Population) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  mutate(max_gdp_pc = max(gdp_pc, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(
    gdp_pc == max_gdp_pc,
    Year >= 1970
  ) |>
  arrange(Year)
```

- Monaco has the highest GDP per capita in the most recent year for which it has data (2016), with Liechtenstein a close second; the two have swapped places several times in recent years.
- These two countries have had the highest GDP per capita for most of the last 50 years.
- Since 1970, the only years where neither Monaco nor Liechtenstein had the highest GDP per capita were 1976 and 1977, when the United Arab Emirates just beat Monaco, and 2017, when Luxembourg is top only because there are no 2017 data for Monaco or Liechtenstein.

# fpp3 3.7, Ex 2

> For each of the following series, make a graph of the data.
> If transforming seems appropriate, do so and describe the effect.

> - United States GDP from `global_economy`
> - Slaughter of Victorian "Bulls, bullocks and steers" in `aus_livestock`
> - Victorian Electricity Demand from `vic_elec`.
> - Gas production from `aus_production`

## United States GDP

```{r}
us_economy <- global_economy |>
  filter(Country == "United States")
us_economy |>
  autoplot(GDP)
```

- Trend appears exponential, a transformation would be useful.

```{r}
us_economy |>
  autoplot(box_cox(GDP, 0))
```

- A log transformation (Box-Cox with $\lambda = 0$) appears slightly too strong.

```{r}
us_economy |>
  autoplot(box_cox(GDP, 0.3))
```

Using $\lambda = 0.3$ looks pretty good, the trend is now almost linear.

Let's see what Guerrero's method suggests.

```{r}
us_economy |>
  features(GDP, features = guerrero)
```

Pretty close to $\lambda = 0.3$, let's see how it looks:

```{r}
us_economy |>
  autoplot(box_cox(GDP, 0.2819714))
```

More or less the same.
Box-Cox transformations are usually insensitive to the choice of $\lambda$.

## Slaughter of Victorian "Bulls, bullocks and steers"

```{r}
vic_bulls <- aus_livestock |>
  filter(State == "Victoria", Animal == "Bulls, bullocks and steers")
vic_bulls |>
  autoplot(Count)
```

- Variation in the series appears to vary slightly with the number of bulls slaughtered in Victoria.
- A transformation may be useful.

```{r}
vic_bulls |>
  autoplot(log(Count))
```

- A log transformation (Box-Cox $\lambda = 0$) appears to normalise most of the variation.
  Let's check with Guerrero's method.

```{r}
vic_bulls |>
  features(Count, features = guerrero)
```

- Pretty close, Guerrero suggests $\lambda = -0.045$.
  This is close enough to zero, so it is probably best to just use a log transformation (allowing better interpretations).

## Victorian Electricity Demand

```{r}
vic_elec |>
  autoplot(Demand)
```

- Seasonal patterns for *time of day* hidden due to density of ink.

- *Day-of-week* seasonality is also hard to see.

- *Time-of-year* seasonality is clear with increasing variance in winter and high skewness in summer.

```{r}
vic_elec |>
  autoplot(box_cox(Demand, 0))
```

- A log transformation makes the variance more even and reduces the skewness.

- Guerrero's method doesn't work here as there are several types of seasonality.

## Australian Gas production

```{r}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(Gas)
```

- Variation in seasonal pattern grows proportionally to the amount of gas produced in Australia.
  A transformation should work well here.

```{r}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(box_cox(Gas, 0))
```

- A log transformation appears slightly too strong, where the variation in periods with smaller gas production is now larger than the variation during greater gas production.

```{r}
aus_production |>
  features(Gas, features = guerrero)
```

- Guerrero's method agrees by selecting a slightly weaker transformation.
  Let's see how it looks.

```{r}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(box_cox(Gas, 0.1095))
```

Looking good!
The variation is now constant across the series.

# fpp3 3.7, Ex 3

> Why is a Box-Cox transformation unhelpful for the `canadian_gas` data?

```{r}
canadian_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Gas production (billion cubic meters)",
    title = "Monthly Canadian gas production"
  )
```

- Here the variation in the series is not proportional to the amount of gas production in Canada.

- When small and large amounts of gas are being produced, we can observe small variation in the seasonal pattern.

- However, between 1975 and 1990 the gas production is moderate, and the variation is large.

- Power transformations (like the Box-Cox transformation) require the variability of the series to vary proportionately to the level of the series.

# fpp3 3.7, Ex 4

> What Box-Cox transformation would you select for your retail data (from Exercise 7 in Section 2.10)?

We use the same series as in Exercise 7 of Section 2.10, omitting the 2018 data.

```{r}
set.seed(12345678)
myseries <- aus_retail |>
  filter(
    `Series ID` == sample(aus_retail$`Series ID`, 1),
    Month < yearmonth("2018 Jan")
  )
myseries |>
  autoplot(Turnover) +
  labs(
    y = "Turnover (million $AUD)",
    x = "Time (Years)",
    title = myseries$Industry[1],
    subtitle = myseries$State[1]
  )
```

The variation appears proportional to the level of the series, so a Box-Cox transformation may be useful.

```{r}
myseries |>
  autoplot(box_cox(Turnover, 0)) +
  labs(
    title = myseries$Industry[1],
    subtitle = myseries$State[1]
  )
```

A log transformation (Box-Cox $\lambda = 0$) appears about right here.
It also makes sense, as retail spending is likely to increase proportionally to population, and therefore the seasonal fluctuations are likely to be proportional to the level of the series.
Logs have the added advantage of being easier to explain than other Box-Cox transformations.

Let's check what the Guerrero method would suggest.

```{r}
myseries |>
  features(Turnover, features = guerrero)
```

Guerrero's method gives $\lambda = 0.08$, which is close to zero, so it supports our choice above.

Note: your series may be different and require a different transformation than what I have used here.

# fpp3 3.7, Ex 5

> For the following series, find an appropriate Box-Cox transformation in order to stabilise the variance.
> Tobacco from `aus_production`, Economy class passengers between Melbourne and Sydney from `ansett`, and Pedestrian counts at Southern Cross Station from `pedestrian`.

## Australian tobacco production

```{r}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(Tobacco)
```

- This variation in this series appears to be mostly constant across different levels of the series.
- If any transformation is required, it would be a weak one.
  This can be seen if a strong transformation (such as log) is used.

```{r}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(log(Tobacco))
```

- Guerrero's method suggests that $\lambda = 0.926$ is appropriate.
  This is a very weak transformation, as it is close to 1 (probably best to not bother transforming this series).

```{r}
aus_production |>
  features(Tobacco, features = guerrero)
```

```{r}
aus_production |>
  autoplot(box_cox(Tobacco, 0.926))
```

- This series appears very similar to the original.
  The transformation is having almost no effect.

## Economy passengers between Melbourne and Sydney

```{r}
ansett |>
  filter(Airports == "MEL-SYD", Class == "Economy") |>
  autoplot(Passengers) +
  labs(title = "Economy passengers", subtitle = "MEL-SYD")
```

- The data does not appear to vary proportionally to the level of the series, so no transformation is needed.

- There are many periods in this time series (such as the strike and change in seat classes) that may need further attention, but this is probably better resolved with modelling rather than transformations.

## Pedestrian counts

```{r}
pedestrian |>
  filter(Sensor == "Southern Cross Station") |>
  autoplot(Count) +
  labs(title = "Southern Cross Pedestrians")
```

- There is a high skewness and some zeros (so we can't take logs).
  Let's try the `log(x+1)` transformation:

```{r}
pedestrian |>
  filter(Sensor == "Southern Cross Station") |>
  autoplot(log1p(Count)) +
  labs(title = "Southern Cross Pedestrians")
```

That's roughly balanced the two tails.

# fpp3 3.7, Ex 9

> Figures 3.18 and 3.19 show the result of decomposing the number of persons in the civilian labour force in Australia each month from February 1978 to August 1995.

> a. Write about 3--5 sentences describing the results of the decomposition.
>    Pay particular attention to the scales of the graphs in making your interpretation.

- The labour force has a steady upward trend, from about 6400 thousand to 9000 thousand, which flattens out during 1991--1992.
- The seasonal component is small relative to the level of the series: it ranges over about $\pm100$ thousand, roughly 1% of the data.
  The panels are drawn on very different scales (compare the grey bars), so the seasonal component looks much larger than it really is.
  December is the highest month, followed by March and September; January and August are the lowest.
- The seasonal pattern changes slowly over time (bottom graph).
  In recent years, March and August have decreased, while July, September and December have increased.
- The remainder is mostly within $\pm50$ thousand, apart from some large negative values in 1991 (down to about $-390$ thousand in March 1991), and a smaller dip in 1993.

> b. Is the recession of 1991/1992 visible in the estimated components?

Yes.
The recession is clearly visible in the remainder component, which has several large negative values in 1991, larger than the seasonal variation.
It is also visible as a flattening of the trend during 1991--1992.
It is not visible in the seasonal component.
Some of the recession has leaked from the trend into the remainder; a smaller trend window would have captured more of it in the trend.

# fpp3 3.7, Ex 10

> This exercise uses the `canadian_gas` data (monthly Canadian gas production in billions of cubic metres, January 1960 -- February 2005).
>
> a. Plot the data using `autoplot()`, `gg_subseries()` and `gg_season()` to look at the effect of the changing seasonality over time.[^1]

[^1]: The evolving seasonal pattern is possibly due to changes in the regulation of gas prices --- thanks to Lewis Kirvan for pointing this out.

```{r}
#| label: gas1

canadian_gas |> autoplot(Volume)
canadian_gas |> gg_subseries(Volume)
canadian_gas |> gg_season(Volume)
```

- The changes in seasonality are possibly due to changes in the regulation of gas prices.

- The time plot shows that the size of the seasonal fluctuations grows from the 1960s to the mid-1980s, and then shrinks again in the 1990s, while the trend has a flat spell in the 1970s and 1980s.
- In the seasonal plot, the early years (orange) have a small seasonal pattern with the highest production in winter (December and January).
  The years in the middle (green and teal) have the largest seasonal swings, with a deep trough in the northern summer, while the most recent years (pink) have a smaller, more irregular pattern.
- The subseries plot is dominated by the trend, so it says little about the changing seasonality.

> b. Do an STL decomposition of the data.
>    You will need to choose a seasonal window to allow for the changing shape of the seasonal component.

```{r}
#| label: gas2

fit <- canadian_gas |>
  model(STL(Volume ~ season(window = 11))) |>
  components()

fit
names(fit)

fit |> autoplot()
```

- A seasonal window of 11 (the default) allows the seasonal shape to evolve smoothly over time.
  Much smaller windows (e.g., 5) over-fit the seasonal component, leaving strong negative autocorrelation at lag 12 in the remainder, while much larger windows (e.g., 21) leave some seasonality in the remainder.

> c. How does the seasonal shape change over time?
>    [Hint: Try plotting the seasonal component using `gg_season()`.]

```{r}
#| label: gas3

fit |> gg_season(season_year)
```

- Here the changes are easier to see.
  Up to about 1990 there is strong seasonality with the greatest volume in the Canadian winter (December and January) and the least in the summer.
- The seasonality increases in size until the mid-1980s, and then decreases.
- After 1990 the seasonality changes shape and appears to be driven partly by the month length, with a sharp dip in February (the shortest month) and smaller dips in June and September (30-day months).

> d. Can you produce a plausible seasonally adjusted series?

```{r}
#| label: gas4

canadian_gas |>
  autoplot(Volume) +
  autolayer(fit, season_adjust, col = "blue")
```

The seasonally adjusted series is plausible: the seasonal fluctuations have been removed, leaving the trend plus some irregular variation, including when the seasonal pattern is changing.

> e. Compare the results with those obtained using SEATS and X-11.
>    How are they different?

```{r}
#| label: gas5

# remember to load library(seasonal) before attempting this question!
canadian_gas |>
  model(X_13ARIMA_SEATS(Volume ~ seats())) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot()
canadian_gas |>
  model(X_13ARIMA_SEATS(Volume ~ x11())) |>
  components() |>
  autoplot()
```

- Both SEATS and X-11 have chosen a multiplicative decomposition here, so their seasonal components are ratios rather than additive effects, and it is hard to compare them directly with the STL results.
  Because the series is at a low level in the 1960s, the multiplicative seasonal component is relatively large at the start of the series, whereas the additive STL seasonal component is small there.
  All three methods show the seasonality shrinking and changing shape after about 1990.

- The SEATS and X-11 seasonal components are very similar to each other.
  Both SEATS and X-11 have estimated a more wiggly trend line than STL.
